claim: The lateral line system enables fishes and aquatic-stage amphibians to detect local water movement via mechanosensory hair cells in neuromasts.
source: The lateral line system enables fishes and aquatic-stage amphibians to detect local water movement via mechanosensory hair cells in neuromasts, and many species to detect weak electric fields via electroreceptors (modified hair cells) in ampullary organs.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about the lateral line system.

claim: Many fish and aquatic-stage amphibian species can detect weak electric fields via electroreceptors (modified hair cells) in ampullary organs.
source: The lateral line system enables fishes and aquatic-stage amphibians to detect local water movement via mechanosensory hair cells in neuromasts, and many species to detect weak electric fields via electroreceptors (modified hair cells) in ampullary organs.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about electroreception.

claim: Both neuromasts and ampullary organs develop from lateral line placodes.
source: Both neuromasts and ampullary organs develop from lateral line placodes, but the molecular mechanisms underpinning ampullary organ formation are understudied relative to neuromasts.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is cited in the introduction.

claim: The molecular mechanisms underpinning ampullary organ formation are understudied relative to neuromasts.
source: Both neuromasts and ampullary organs develop from lateral line placodes, but the molecular mechanisms underpinning ampullary organ formation are understudied relative to neuromasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the state of the literature, as the authors note that model organisms like zebrafish and Xenopus lack electroreception.

claim: The ancestral lineages of zebrafish (teleosts) and Xenopus (frogs) independently lost electroreception.
source: This is because the ancestral lineages of zebrafish (teleosts) and Xenopus (frogs) independently lost electroreception.
evidence: This is established knowledge in evolutionary biology, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Bmp5 was identified as a promising candidate gene via differential RNA-seq in the Mississippi paddlefish (Polyodon spathula).
source: We identified Bmp5 as a promising candidate via differential RNA-seq in an electroreceptive ray-finned fish, the Mississippi paddlefish (Polyodon spathula; Modrell et al., 2017, eLife 6: e24197).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a previous publication by the authors (Modrell et al., 2017).

claim: Bmp5 and four other Bmp pathway genes are expressed in the developing lateral line of sterlet sturgeon (Acipenser ruthenus).
source: In an experimentally tractable relative, the sterlet sturgeon (Acipenser ruthenus), we found that Bmp5 and four other Bmp pathway genes are expressed in the developing lateral line, and that Bmp signalling is active.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript (Figures 1, 3, and supplements).

claim: Bmp signalling is active in the developing lateral line of sterlet sturgeon.
source: In an experimentally tractable relative, the sterlet sturgeon (Acipenser ruthenus), we found that Bmp5 and four other Bmp pathway genes are expressed in the developing lateral line, and that Bmp signalling is active.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity (Figure 2).

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis targeting Bmp5 in G0-injected sterlet embryos resulted in fewer ampullary organs.
source: Furthermore, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis targeting Bmp5 in G0-injected sterlet embryos resulted in fewer ampullary organs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRISPR/Cas9 experiments presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: When Bmp signalling was inhibited by DMH1 treatment shortly before the formation of ampullary organ primordia, supernumerary ampullary organs developed.
source: Conversely, when Bmp signalling was inhibited by DMH1 treatment shortly before the formation of ampullary organ primordia, supernumerary ampullary organs developed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from DMH1 treatment experiments presented in Figures 6, 7, and 8.

claim: Bmp5 promotes ampullary organ development.
source: These data suggest that Bmp5 promotes ampullary organ development, whereas Bmp signalling via another ligand(s) prevents their overproduction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CRISPR/Cas9 data showing fewer ampullary organs when Bmp5 is disrupted.

claim: Bmp signalling via another ligand(s) prevents overproduction of ampullary organs.
source: These data suggest that Bmp5 promotes ampullary organ development, whereas Bmp signalling via another ligand(s) prevents their overproduction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DMH1 treatment data showing supernumerary ampullary organs when Bmp signalling is broadly inhibited.

claim: Bmp signalling has opposing roles during ampullary organ formation.
source: Taken together, this demonstrates opposing roles for Bmp signalling during ampullary organ formation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, synthesizing the CRISPR and DMH1 treatment data.

claim: The lateral line system is an evolutionarily ancient sensory system found in fishes and aquatic-stage amphibians.
source: The lateral line system is an evolutionarily ancient sensory system found in fishes and aquatic-stage amphibians (Bullock et al., 1983; Northcutt, 1997; Mogdans, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Neuromasts detect local water movement via mechanosensory hair cells whose apical surfaces are embedded in a gelatinous cupula.
source: Neuromasts, arranged in characteristic lines across the head and trunk, detect local water movement via mechanosensory hair cells ('touch at a distance') whose apical surfaces are embedded in a gelatinous cupula (Cernuda-Cernuda and García-Fernández, 1996; Montgomery et al., 2014; Pickett and Raible, 2019; Mogdans, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In non-teleost electroreceptive fishes and amphibians, fields of electrosensory ampullary organs flank some or all of the neuromast lines on the head.
source: In non-teleost electroreceptive fishes and amphibians, fields of electrosensory ampullary organs flank some or all of the neuromast lines on the head (Bullock et al., 1983; Baker et al., 2013; Crampton, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The electrosensory division of the lateral line system was independently lost in several lineages, including those leading to frogs/toads and to teleost fishes.
source: The electrosensory division of the lateral line system was independently lost in several lineages, for example, those leading to frogs/toads and to teleost fishes (although electroreception with physiologically distinct electroreceptors independently evolved multiple times in a few groups of teleost fishes) (Bullock et al., 1983; Baker et al., 2013; Crampton, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Electroreception with physiologically distinct electroreceptors independently evolved multiple times in a few groups of teleost fishes.
source: The electrosensory division of the lateral line system was independently lost in several lineages, for example, those leading to frogs/toads and to teleost fishes (although electroreception with physiologically distinct electroreceptors independently evolved multiple times in a few groups of teleost fishes) (Bullock et al., 1983; Baker et al., 2013; Crampton, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Salamanders (for example, the axolotl) are electroreceptive.
source: Although salamanders (for example, the axolotl) are electroreceptive, the primary anamniote lab models, Xenopus and zebrafish, as well as other lab model teleosts such as medaka and cavefish, only have the mechanosensory division.
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Xenopus and zebrafish, as well as other lab model teleosts such as medaka and cavefish, only have the mechanosensory division of the lateral line system.
source: Although salamanders (for example, the axolotl) are electroreceptive, the primary anamniote lab models, Xenopus and zebrafish, as well as other lab model teleosts such as medaka and cavefish, only have the mechanosensory division.
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Non-teleost ampullary organs have a 'flask-shaped' chamber with a sensory epithelium at the base, connected to a pore in the epidermis via a canal filled with an electrically conductive jelly.
source: Non-teleost ampullary organs have a 'flask-shaped' chamber with a sensory epithelium at the base, connected to a pore in the epidermis via a canal filled with an electrically conductive jelly (Jørgensen, 2011; Josberger et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Ampullary electroreceptor cells are modified hair cells.
source: Ampullary electroreceptor cells are modified hair cells (Jørgensen, 2005; Baker and Modrell, 2018; Baker, 2019) that respond to weak cathodal (exterior-negative) electric fields, primarily for detecting prey or avoiding predators (Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; Crampton, 2019; Leitch and Julius, 2019; Chagnaud et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Ampullary electroreceptor cells respond to weak cathodal (exterior-negative) electric fields, primarily for detecting prey or avoiding predators.
source: Ampullary electroreceptor cells are modified hair cells (Jørgensen, 2005; Baker and Modrell, 2018; Baker, 2019) that respond to weak cathodal (exterior-negative) electric fields, primarily for detecting prey or avoiding predators (Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; Crampton, 2019; Leitch and Julius, 2019; Chagnaud et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Both neuromasts and ampullary organs contain several types of support cells that flank the sensory receptor cells.
source: Both neuromasts and ampullary organs contain several types of support cells that flank the sensory receptor cells: these have a range of support functions including secretion (see, for example, Cernuda-Cernuda and García-Fernández, 1996; Camacho et al., 2007; Russell et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In zebrafish neuromasts, both active and quiescent stem cell populations have been identified amongst the various support cell populations.
source: In zebrafish neuromasts, both active and quiescent stem cell populations have been identified amongst the various support cell populations, which differentiate into hair cells during homeostasis and after injury (see Lush and Piotrowski, 2014; Lush et al., 2019; Undurraga et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Support cell populations in zebrafish neuromasts differentiate into hair cells during homeostasis and after injury.
source: In zebrafish neuromasts, both active and quiescent stem cell populations have been identified amongst the various support cell populations, which differentiate into hair cells during homeostasis and after injury (see Lush and Piotrowski, 2014; Lush et al., 2019; Undurraga et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Neuromasts, ampullary organs and their afferent neurons all develop from a series of lateral line placodes on the head.
source: Neuromasts, ampullary organs and their afferent neurons all develop from a series of lateral line placodes (thickened patches of neurogenic ectoderm) on the head (Northcutt, 1997; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Baker, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: There are six bilateral pairs of lateral line placodes.
source: There are six bilateral pairs of lateral line placodes: the anterodorsal, anteroventral and otic lateral line placodes form rostral to the otic vesicle, whereas the middle, supratemporal and posterior lateral line placodes form caudal to the otic vesicle (Northcutt, 1997; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Baker, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The anterodorsal, anteroventral and otic lateral line placodes form rostral to the otic vesicle.
source: There are six bilateral pairs of lateral line placodes: the anterodorsal, anteroventral and otic lateral line placodes form rostral to the otic vesicle, whereas the middle, supratemporal and posterior lateral line placodes form caudal to the otic vesicle (Northcutt, 1997; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Baker, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The middle, supratemporal and posterior lateral line placodes form caudal to the otic vesicle.
source: There are six bilateral pairs of lateral line placodes: the anterodorsal, anteroventral and otic lateral line placodes form rostral to the otic vesicle, whereas the middle, supratemporal and posterior lateral line placodes form caudal to the otic vesicle (Northcutt, 1997; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Baker, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Neuroblasts delaminate from the pole of each lateral line placode lying closest to the otic vesicle.
source: Neuroblasts delaminate from the pole of each placode lying closest to the otic vesicle; they form afferent bipolar neurons (which coalesce in lateral line ganglia) whose peripheral axons accompany the placode as it continues to develop and form sensory organs (see Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; McGraw et al., 2017; Chitnis, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Neuroblasts from lateral line placodes form afferent bipolar neurons which coalesce in lateral line ganglia.
source: Neuroblasts delaminate from the pole of each placode lying closest to the otic vesicle; they form afferent bipolar neurons (which coalesce in lateral line ganglia) whose peripheral axons accompany the placode as it continues to develop and form sensory organs (see Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; McGraw et al., 2017; Chitnis, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Peripheral axons of lateral line afferent neurons accompany the placode as it continues to develop and form sensory organs.
source: Neuroblasts delaminate from the pole of each placode lying closest to the otic vesicle; they form afferent bipolar neurons (which coalesce in lateral line ganglia) whose peripheral axons accompany the placode as it continues to develop and form sensory organs (see Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; McGraw et al., 2017; Chitnis, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Neuromasts on the trunk originate from the posterior lateral line placode.
source: Neuromasts on the trunk originate from the posterior lateral line placode, whose development has been most intensively studied in the teleost zebrafish (see, for example, Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; McGraw et al., 2017; Chitnis, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The posterior lateral line placode gives rise to an early-migrating primordium (primI) that migrates as a cell-collective along the trunk, depositing neuromasts and a line of interneuromast cells.
source: Initially, it gives rise to an early-migrating primordium (primI) that migrates as a cell-collective along the trunk, depositing neuromasts and a line of interneuromast cells that act as progenitors for later-forming neuromasts (reviewed by Piotrowski and Baker, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Interneuromast cells deposited by primI act as progenitors for later-forming neuromasts.
source: Initially, it gives rise to an early-migrating primordium (primI) that migrates as a cell-collective along the trunk, depositing neuromasts and a line of interneuromast cells that act as progenitors for later-forming neuromasts (reviewed by Piotrowski and Baker, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: A day after primI, another placode develops in the same position, which gives rise to two primordia: primD and primII.
source: A day later, another placode develops in the same position, which gives rise to two primordia: primD migrates dorsally to give rise to a dorsal line of neuromasts; the other (primII) migrates along the same pathway as primI, depositing secondary neuromasts in between the primary neuromasts left behind by primI (reviewed by Piotrowski and Baker, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: PrimD migrates dorsally to give rise to a dorsal line of neuromasts.
source: A day later, another placode develops in the same position, which gives rise to two primordia: primD migrates dorsally to give rise to a dorsal line of neuromasts; the other (primII) migrates along the same pathway as primI, depositing secondary neuromasts in between the primary neuromasts left behind by primI (reviewed by Piotrowski and Baker, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: PrimII migrates along the same pathway as primI, depositing secondary neuromasts in between the primary neuromasts left behind by primI.
source: A day later, another placode develops in the same position, which gives rise to two primordia: primD migrates dorsally to give rise to a dorsal line of neuromasts; the other (primII) migrates along the same pathway as primI, depositing secondary neuromasts in between the primary neuromasts left behind by primI (reviewed by Piotrowski and Baker, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The migrating posterior lateral line primordium is closely followed by the growth cones of afferent lateral line axons and their associated Schwann cells.
source: The migrating posterior lateral line primordium is closely followed by the growth cones of afferent lateral line axons and their associated Schwann cells (Metcalfe, 1985; Gilmour et al., 2002; Gilmour et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In non-teleosts, lateral line placodes do not migrate, but rather elongate over the head to form sensory ridges that eventually fragment, leaving a line of neuromasts along the centre of the ridge.
source: In non-teleosts, the other lateral line placodes do not migrate, but rather elongate over the head to form sensory ridges that eventually fragment, leaving a line of neuromasts along the centre of the ridge (see Winklbauer, 1989; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In electroreceptive species, ampullary organs form later than neuromasts, in fields flanking the line of neuromasts.
source: In electroreceptive species, ampullary organs form later than neuromasts, in fields flanking the line of neuromasts (Northcutt, 2005; Baker et al., 2013; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In elongating lateral line primordia, afferent axons and associated Schwann cells accompany the primordia.
source: Just as in the migrating posterior lateral line primordium, afferent axons and associated Schwann cells accompany the elongating primordia (Winklbauer, 1989; Northcutt, 2005; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The Mississippi paddlefish (Polyodon spathula) has more ampullary organs than any other species.
source: Given the loss of electroreception in the lineages leading to frogs/toads and teleosts, we used a chondrostean ray-finned fish, the Mississippi paddlefish (Polyodon spathula), which has more ampullary organs than any other species (Chagnaud et al., 2021), as a model to study ampullary organ development (Modrell et al., 2011a; Modrell et al., 2011b; Modrell et al., 2017a; Modrell et al., 2017b; Minařík et al., 2024a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: A differential bulk RNA-seq screen at late-larval stages in paddlefish, comparing gene expression in fin tissue versus operculum tissue, resulted in a lateral line-enriched gene-set containing almost 500 candidate genes enriched by at least twofold.
source: To identify candidate genes potentially involved in ampullary organ development, we performed a differential bulk RNA-seq screen at late-larval stages, comparing gene expression in fin tissue (which lacks lateral line organs) versus operculum tissue (which has many ampullary organs and some neuromasts). This resulted in a lateral line-enriched gene-set containing almost 500 candidate genes enriched by at least twofold in paddlefish opercular versus fin tissue (Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: Expression analysis of candidate genes from the paddlefish lateral line-enriched dataset suggested that electroreceptors are closely related to hair cells and that the mechanisms underlying their development are highly conserved.
source: Expression analysis of a range of candidate genes from this dataset and other candidates important for hair cell development (Modrell et al., 2017a; Modrell et al., 2017b; Minařík et al., 2024a), together with small-molecule manipulation of the Fgf and Notch signalling pathways (Modrell et al., 2017b), suggested that electoreceptors are closely related to hair cells and that the mechanisms underlying their development are highly conserved.
evidence: This statement is supported by data from previous publications by the authors.

claim: The sterlet (Acipenser ruthenus) is a more experimentally tractable chondrostean with a much longer spawning season than the paddlefish.
source: To enable further investigation of gene function in ampullary organ and electroreceptor development, we moved to a more experimentally tractable chondrostean with a much longer spawning season: a small sturgeon, the sterlet (Acipenser ruthenus).
evidence: This is a statement about the practical advantages of using sterlet as a model organism.

claim: Investigation of additional candidate genes from the paddlefish lateral line-enriched dataset in paddlefish and sterlet identified both mechanosensory-restricted and electrosensory-restricted transcription factor gene expression.
source: Investigation of additional candidate genes from the paddlefish lateral line-enriched dataset in paddlefish and sterlet identified both mechanosensory-restricted and electrosensory-restricted transcription factor gene expression (Modrell et al., 2017a; Minařík et al., 2024a).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from previous publications by the authors.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis in G0-injected sterlet embryos identified a conserved requirement for the 'hair cell' transcription factor Atoh1 in electroreceptor formation.
source: We recently used CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis in G0-injected sterlet embryos to identify a conserved requirement for the 'hair cell' transcription factor Atoh1 in electroceptor formation and identified a role for mechanosensory-restricted Foxg1 in blocking ampullary organ formation within neuromast lines (preprint, Minařík et al., 2024b).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from a recent preprint by the authors.

claim: Mechanosensory-restricted Foxg1 blocks ampullary organ formation within neuromast lines.
source: We recently used CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis in G0-injected sterlet embryos to identify a conserved requirement for the 'hair cell' transcription factor Atoh1 in electroceptor formation and identified a role for mechanosensory-restricted Foxg1 in blocking ampullary organ formation within neuromast lines (preprint, Minařík et al., 2024b).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from a recent preprint by the authors.

claim: Bmp5 was 2.5-fold enriched in late-larval paddlefish operculum versus fin tissue.
source: One gene present in the paddlefish lateral line-enriched gene set was the Bmp ligand gene Bmp5 (2.5-fold enriched in late-larval paddlefish operculum versus fin tissue; Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: At stage 37, faint Bmp5 expression was seen within developing gill filaments but there was no detectable lateral line expression in sterlet.
source: At stage 37, faint Bmp5 expression was seen within developing gill filaments but there was no detectable lateral line expression (Figure 1A and B), despite the presence of some differentiated neuromasts (i.e., with Cacna1d-expressing hair cells; Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: At stage 37, some differentiated neuromasts with Cacna1d-expressing hair cells are present in sterlet.
source: At stage 37, faint Bmp5 expression was seen within developing gill filaments but there was no detectable lateral line expression (Figure 1A and B), despite the presence of some differentiated neuromasts (i.e., with Cacna1d-expressing hair cells; Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: By stage 40, strong Bmp5 expression was visible in mature neuromasts as well as ampullary organ primordia in sterlet.
source: By stage 40, strong Bmp5 expression was visible in mature neuromasts as well as ampullary organ primordia (Figure 1E and F; compare with Cacna1d expression in Figure 1G and H, which shows that few electroreceptors have differentiated at this stage).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: At stage 40, few electroreceptors have differentiated in sterlet.
source: By stage 40, strong Bmp5 expression was visible in mature neuromasts as well as ampullary organ primordia (Figure 1E and F; compare with Cacna1d expression in Figure 1G and H, which shows that few electroreceptors have differentiated at this stage).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: At stage 42, Bmp5 expression was seen in mature ampullary organs but seemed weaker in neuromasts in sterlet.
source: At stage 42, Bmp5 expression was seen in mature ampullary organs but seemed weaker in neuromasts (Figure 1I and J; compare with Cacna1d expression in Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: By stage 45, Bmp5 expression persisted in ampullary organs, although this seemed weaker than at stage 40, and was no longer seen in most neuromasts on the head in sterlet.
source: By stage 45, Bmp5 expression persisted in ampullary organs, although this seemed weaker than at stage 40, and was no longer seen in most neuromasts on the head (Figure 1M and N; compare with Cacna1d expression in Figure 1O and P).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1M and N.

claim: On the trunk at stage 45, Bmp5 expression was seen in a subset of regularly spaced neuromasts in the main body line, as well as the dorsal line deposited by primD, with stronger expression in more rostral (i.e., earlier-deposited) neuromasts in sterlet.
source: On the trunk, Bmp5 expression was seen in a subset of regularly spaced neuromasts in the main body line, as well as the dorsal line deposited by primD, with stronger expression in more rostral (i.e., earlier-deposited) neuromasts (Figure 1Q; compare with Cacna1d expression in all trunk neuromasts in Figure 1R).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1Q.

claim: The Bmp5-expressing neuromasts in the main body line at stage 45 are secondary neuromasts deposited by the later-migrating primII, which are offset slightly dorsally to those deposited earlier by primI.
source: The Bmp5-expressing neuromasts in the main body line are secondary neuromasts deposited by the later-migrating primII, which are offset slightly dorsally to those deposited earlier by primI, which are Bmp5-negative (compare with Cacna1d expression in Figure 1R; examples of primII-deposited neuromasts are highlighted).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1Q and R.

claim: Bmp5 is expressed early within ampullary organ primordia and maintained in mature ampullary organs at least through to the onset of independent feeding at stage 45 in sterlet.
source: Overall, these results suggest that Bmp5 is expressed early within ampullary organ primordia and maintained in mature ampullary organs at least through to the onset of independent feeding at stage 45.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Bmp5 is only expressed in mature neuromasts in sterlet, after the onset of hair cell differentiation, and then only transiently.
source: In contrast, Bmp5 only seems to be expressed in mature neuromasts, after the onset of hair cell differentiation, and then only transiently.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: At stage 30, faint pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was seen in the region of the anteroventral lateral line primordium in sterlet.
source: At stage 30 (the earliest stage examined), faint pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was seen in the region of the anteroventral lateral line primordium (Figure 2A and B; compare with Sox2 immunoreactivity at stage 32 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B; Sox2 is expressed in lateral line primordia and maintained in supporting cells; Hernández et al., 2007; Modrell et al., 2017a; Minařík et al., 2024a).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Sox2 is expressed in lateral line primordia and maintained in supporting cells.
source: At stage 30 (the earliest stage examined), faint pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was seen in the region of the anteroventral lateral line primordium (Figure 2A and B; compare with Sox2 immunoreactivity at stage 32 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B; Sox2 is expressed in lateral line primordia and maintained in supporting cells; Hernández et al., 2007; Modrell et al., 2017a; Minařík et al., 2024a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: By stage 34, pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was detectable in lateral line primordia, with a ring pattern around developing neuromast primordia in the otic/anterodorsal and anteroventral primordia in sterlet.
source: By stage 34, pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was detectable in lateral line primordia, with a ring pattern around developing neuromast primordia in the otic/anterodorsal and anteroventral primordia (Figure 2C and D; compare with stage 35 Sox2 expression in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The first Cacna1d-positive differentiated hair cells are seen in the otic/anterodorsal and anteroventral primordia region at stage 35 in sterlet.
source: (The first Cacna1d-positive differentiated hair cells are seen in this region at stage 35; Minařík et al., 2024a.)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous publication by the authors.

claim: At stage 36, weak pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was still seen around developing neuromasts in sterlet.
source: At stage 36 (Figure 2E and F), weak pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was still seen around developing neuromasts (compare with stage 37 Cacna1d expression in Figure 1C and D; stage 37 Sox2 immunoreactivity in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F), but we were intrigued to see more prominent immunoreactivity in a filamentous pattern that seemed most likely to correspond to lateral line nerves (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: At stage 36, more prominent pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was seen in a filamentous pattern that seemed most likely to correspond to lateral line nerves in sterlet.
source: At stage 36 (Figure 2E and F), weak pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was still seen around developing neuromasts (compare with stage 37 Cacna1d expression in Figure 1C and D; stage 37 Sox2 immunoreactivity in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F), but we were intrigued to see more prominent immunoreactivity in a filamentous pattern that seemed most likely to correspond to lateral line nerves (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2E and F, and is an inference about the identity of the labeled structures.

claim: The filamentous pattern of pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity continued at stages 38 and 40 in sterlet.
source: This pattern continued at stages 38 and 40 (Figure 2G–J); indeed pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactive collaterals seemed to be developing from the infraorbital nerve between stages 38 and 40 (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2G-J.

claim: pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactive collaterals seemed to be developing from the infraorbital nerve between stages 38 and 40 in sterlet.
source: This pattern continued at stages 38 and 40 (Figure 2G–J); indeed pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactive collaterals seemed to be developing from the infraorbital nerve between stages 38 and 40 (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2G-J, and is an inference about the developmental process.

claim: At stage 40, diffuse pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was also seen in regions flanking the nerves where ampullary organ primordia are forming in sterlet.
source: At stage 40, diffuse immunoreactivity was also seen in regions flanking the nerves where ampullary organ primordia are forming (Figure 2I and J; compare with stage 40 Bmp5 expression in Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: Strong pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was seen in the barbel primordia, around the nares and mouth, in gill filaments, and between stages 36 and 40 in a patch between the barbels and the otic vesicle that likely represents a muscle, the m. protractor hyomandibulae, in sterlet.
source: (Strong pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was also seen in the barbel primordia, around the nares and mouth, in gill filaments, and between stages 36 and 40 in a patch between the barbels and the otic vesicle that likely represents a muscle, the m. protractor hyomandibulae; Warth et al., 2018.)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2, and the identification of the muscle is supported by a citation.

claim: By stage 42, pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was visible in ampullary organs and much less prominent in lateral line nerves in sterlet.
source: By stage 42, pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was visible in ampullary organs and much less prominent in lateral line nerves (Figure 2K and L; compare with stage 42 Sox2 expression in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2K and L.

claim: At stages 43 and 45, pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was more clearly visible in neuromasts as well as ampullary organs, in all cases at the periphery rather than centre of each organ in sterlet.
source: At stages 43 and 45, pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was more clearly visible in neuromasts as well as ampullary organs, in all cases at the periphery rather than centre of each organ (Figure 2M–P; compare with the hair cell/electroreceptor marker Cacna1d at stage 42 in Figure 1K and L and at stage 45 in Figure 1O and P, and the supporting cell marker Sox2 at stages 42 and 45 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2M-P.

claim: The peripheral pattern of pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity suggests that Bmp signalling is active in supporting cells rather than receptor cells in sterlet.
source: This peripheral pattern of pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity suggests that Bmp signalling is active in supporting cells rather than receptor cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunohistochemistry data and the known locations of supporting cells versus receptor cells.

claim: At stages 43 and 45, pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity on the head seemed to be particularly strong in the supraorbital and infraorbital neuromast lines in sterlet.
source: Also at stages 43 and 45, we noted that pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity on the head seemed to be particularly strong in the supraorbital and infraorbital neuromast lines (compare with Sox2 expression at stages 42 and 45 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2M-P.

claim: At stage 39, pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was seen in primI and a diffuse but somewhat continuous line trailing behind it, as well as in primII, which is located much further rostrally and a little dorsal to the main line in sterlet.
source: At stage 39, pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was seen in primI and a diffuse but somewhat continuous line trailing behind it, as well as in primII, which is located much further rostrally and a little dorsal to the main line (Figure 2Q; compare with Sox2 expression in Figure 2R).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2Q.

claim: At stage 45, strong pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was seen in primII and primD, and more weakly along the path taken by primII, with increased intensity at the periphery of the primII-deposited neuromasts in sterlet.
source: At stage 45, strong pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was seen in primII and primD, and more weakly along the path taken by primII, with increased intensity at the periphery of the primII-deposited neuromasts (Figure 2S; compare with Sox2 expression in all neuromasts in Figure 2T and with Bmp5 expression in primII-deposited neuromasts in Figure 1Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2S.

claim: Bmp signalling is active throughout lateral line development in the sterlet, including lateral line organ primordia and even lateral line nerves, and later at the periphery (rather than the centre) of maturing ampullary organs and neuromasts.
source: Overall, these data suggest that Bmp signalling is active throughout lateral line development in the sterlet, including lateral line organ primordia and even lateral line nerves, and later at the periphery (rather than the centre) of maturing ampullary organs and neuromasts, suggesting activity in supporting cells rather than receptor cells.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Bmp signalling activity at the periphery of maturing ampullary organs and neuromasts suggests activity in supporting cells rather than receptor cells in sterlet.
source: Overall, these data suggest that Bmp signalling is active throughout lateral line development in the sterlet, including lateral line organ primordia and even lateral line nerves, and later at the periphery (rather than the centre) of maturing ampullary organs and neuromasts, suggesting activity in supporting cells rather than receptor cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunohistochemistry data and the known locations of supporting cells versus receptor cells.

claim: Bmp5 was the only gene encoding a Bmp ligand or receptor in the late-larval paddlefish lateral line-enriched gene-set.
source: Bmp5 was the only gene encoding a Bmp ligand or receptor in the late-larval paddlefish lateral line-enriched gene-set (Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: The timecourse and pattern of pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity in the developing sterlet lateral line system was more extensive than Bmp5 expression, suggesting other Bmp ligands must be expressed.
source: However, the timecourse and pattern of pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity in the developing sterlet lateral line system was more extensive than Bmp5 expression (compare Figure 1 and Figure 2), suggesting other Bmp ligands must be expressed that were not enriched in the transcriptome of late-larval paddlefish operculum versus fin tissue (Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the Bmp5 expression data (Figure 1) with the pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity data (Figure 2).

claim: Bmp4 expression was not evident in the developing sterlet lateral line at stage 37 or stage 38.
source: Bmp4 expression was not evident in the developing sterlet lateral line at stage 37 or stage 38 (Figure 3A–D); the very faint expression in two widely spaced dorsal patches at stage 38 may be sensory patches in the otic vesicle (Figure 3C and D), or may represent early-forming neuromast primordia in the otic and supratemporal lines (see Gibbs and Northcutt, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: The very faint Bmp4 expression in two widely spaced dorsal patches at stage 38 may be sensory patches in the otic vesicle, or may represent early-forming neuromast primordia in the otic and supratemporal lines in sterlet.
source: Bmp4 expression was not evident in the developing sterlet lateral line at stage 37 or stage 38 (Figure 3A–D); the very faint expression in two widely spaced dorsal patches at stage 38 may be sensory patches in the otic vesicle (Figure 3C and D), or may represent early-forming neuromast primordia in the otic and supratemporal lines (see Gibbs and Northcutt, 2004).
evidence: This is speculation about the identity of the Bmp4-expressing structures, supported by a citation.

claim: Stronger Bmp4 expression was seen in fin, barbel and gill filament primordia, and around the nares at stages 37 and 38 in sterlet.
source: Stronger expression was also seen in fin, barbel and gill filament primordia, and around the nares (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: By stage 40, diffuse Bmp4 expression was observed in neuromast regions and fields of ampullary organ primordia on the head in sterlet.
source: By stage 40, diffuse Bmp4 expression was observed in neuromast regions and fields of ampullary organ primordia on the head (Figure 3E and F; compare with Bmp5 and Cacna1d expression in Figure 1E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: At stage 40, stronger Bmp4 expression was seen on the trunk in primI, with much weaker expression in the most recently deposited neuromasts near to the primordium, plus a spot that most likely represents primII in sterlet.
source: Stronger expression was also seen on the trunk in primI, with much weaker expression in the most recently deposited neuromasts near to the primordium, plus a spot that most likely represents primII (Figure 3G; compare with stage 40 Sox2 expression on the trunk in Figure 2—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3G, and the identification of primII is an inference.

claim: At stage 42, Bmp4 expression in lateral line regions on the head was almost gone, with only faint expression remaining in the dorsal infraorbital ampullary organ field, just below the eye in sterlet.
source: At stage 42, Bmp4 expression in lateral line regions on the head was almost gone, with only faint expression remaining in the dorsal infraorbital ampullary organ field, just below the eye (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: At stage 42, strong Bmp4 expression was seen in primII and primD on the trunk in sterlet.
source: However, strong expression was seen in primII and primD on the trunk (Figure 3J; compare with stage 42 Sox2 expression in Figure 2—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: By stage 45, Bmp4 was no longer expressed in lateral line regions on the head, although expression remained in the barbels and gills in sterlet.
source: By stage 45, Bmp4 was no longer expressed in lateral line regions on the head, although expression remained in the barbels and gills (Figure 3K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3K-L.

claim: At stage 45, the migrating lateral line primordia on the trunk still expressed Bmp4 in sterlet.
source: As at stages 40 and 42, the migrating lateral line primordia on the trunk still expressed Bmp4 at stage 45 (Figure 3M; compare with stage 45 Sox2 expression in Figure 2—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Bmp4 plays a more transient role than Bmp5 in lateral line organ development in sterlet.
source: These data suggest that Bmp4 plays a more transient role than Bmp5 in lateral line organ development.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the Bmp4 expression data (Figure 3) with the Bmp5 expression data (Figure 1).

claim: An as-yet unidentified Bmp ligand gene is most likely expressed in lateral line primordia before either Bmp5 or Bmp4 in sterlet.
source: Furthermore, most likely an as-yet unidentified Bmp ligand gene is expressed in lateral line primordia before either Bmp5 or Bmp4, given that pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity was detectable in lateral line primordia at stage 34 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity data (Figure 2C and D) and the absence of Bmp5 and Bmp4 expression at that stage.

claim: Acvr2a encodes ActRIIA (activin A receptor type 2 A), a type II Bmp receptor that promiscuously binds multiple ligands including Bmp5 and Bmp4.
source: The only Bmp receptor gene we examined was Acvr2a, encoding ActRIIA (activin A receptor type 2 A), a type II Bmp receptor that promiscuously binds multiple ligands including Bmp5 and Bmp4 (Yadin et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Acvr2a was not expressed at stage 37 in sterlet, so other receptors must be involved in mediating Bmp signalling in lateral line primordia at this and earlier stages.
source: Acvr2a was not expressed at stage 37 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), so other receptors must be involved in mediating Bmp signalling in lateral line primordia at this and earlier stages (see, for example, pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity at stage 34 and stage 36; Figure 2C–F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of Acvr2a expression at stage 37 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) and the presence of pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity at earlier stages (Figure 2C-F).

claim: By stage 38, Acvr2a expression was detectable in developing neuromast regions in sterlet, although background levels were high.
source: By stage 38, although background levels were high, Acvr2a expression was detectable in developing neuromast regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: By stage 40, Acvr2a was expressed at the periphery of ampullary organ primordia and neuromasts on the head in sterlet.
source: By stage 40, Acvr2a was expressed at the periphery of ampullary organ primordia and neuromasts on the head (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F; compare with stage 40 Bmp5 and Cacna1d expression in Figure 1E–H, and with stage 39 Sox2 expression in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: At stage 40, Acvr2a was expressed in primI and a trailing line of cells behind it, plus a spot most likely representing primII in sterlet.
source: Also at stage 40, Acvr2a was expressed in primI and a trailing line of cells behind it, plus a spot most likely representing primII (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, and the identification of primII is an inference.

claim: At stage 42, Acvr2a expression persisted in both the head and trunk, with expression now also seen in primD and in the rostral trunk neuromasts deposited by primII in sterlet.
source: This pattern persisted in both the head and trunk at stage 42, with expression now also seen primD and in the rostral trunk neuromasts deposited by primII (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H-J.

claim: By stage 45, Acvr2a expression appeared to be fading on the head, with only faint expression at the periphery of ampullary organs in a few areas in sterlet.
source: By stage 45, Acvr2a expression appeared to be fading on the head, with only faint expression at the periphery of ampullary organs in a few areas (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K and L.

claim: At stage 45, Acvr2a expression continued in the trunk neuromast lines in sterlet.
source: However, expression continued in the trunk neuromast lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1M.

claim: The Acvr2a expression pattern does not fully complement either Bmp5 or Bmp4 expression, or pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity, suggesting other type II receptor(s), as well as type I receptors, must be involved in sterlet.
source: Overall, the Acvr2a expression pattern does not fully complement either Bmp5 or Bmp4 expression (compare with Figure 1 and Figure 3, respectively), or pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity (Figure 2). Hence, other type II receptor(s), as well of course as type I receptors, must be involved.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the Acvr2a expression data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with the Bmp5 expression data (Figure 1), Bmp4 expression data (Figure 3), and pSMAD1/5/9 immunoreactivity data (Figure 2).

claim: Three genes encoding secreted Bmp inhibitors were present in the late-larval paddlefish lateral line-enriched gene-set: Sostdc1, Apcdd1 and Vwc2.
source: Three genes encoding secreted Bmp inhibitors were present in the late-larval paddlefish lateral line-enriched gene-set (Modrell et al., 2017a): Sostdc1, Apcdd1 and Vwc2.
evidence: This statement is supported by data from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: Vwc2 was 4.5-fold lateral line-enriched in the late-larval paddlefish lateral line-enriched gene-set.
source: Vwc2 was 4.5-fold lateral line-enriched (Modrell et al., 2017a), but ISH for this gene in sterlet was unsuccessful so it is not considered further.
evidence: This statement is supported by data from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: Sostdc1 (sclerostin domain-containing 1; also known as Wise, Ectodin) is a secreted antagonist of both the Bmp and Wnt pathways.
source: Sostdc1 (sclerostin domain-containing 1; also known as Wise, Ectodin) is a secreted antagonist of both the Bmp and Wnt pathways (Tong et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Sostdc1 was 4.2-fold enriched in late-larval paddlefish operculum versus fin tissue.
source: Sostdc1 was 4.2-fold enriched in late-larval paddlefish operculum versus fin tissue (Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: From stage 36 onwards, Sostdc1 expression was seen in lines of differentiated neuromasts (and in gill filament primordia) on the head in sterlet.
source: From stage 36 onwards, Sostdc1 expression was seen in lines of differentiated neuromasts (and in gill filament primordia) on the head, and from stage 40 onwards, in the migrating primordia and neuromasts on the trunk (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–M; compare with Cacna1d expression in Figure 1 and Sox2 expression in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-P).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-M.

claim: From stage 40 onwards, Sostdc1 expression was seen in the migrating primordia and neuromasts on the trunk in sterlet.
source: From stage 36 onwards, Sostdc1 expression was seen in lines of differentiated neuromasts (and in gill filament primordia) on the head, and from stage 40 onwards, in the migrating primordia and neuromasts on the trunk (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–M; compare with Cacna1d expression in Figure 1 and Sox2 expression in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-P).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-M.

claim: At stage 42, Sostdc1 expression was also detected in ampullary organs in sterlet.
source: At stage 42, Sostdc1 expression was also detected in ampullary organs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H and I), but this had already disappeared by stage 45 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H and I.

claim: Sostdc1 expression in ampullary organs had already disappeared by stage 45 in sterlet.
source: At stage 42, Sostdc1 expression was also detected in ampullary organs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H and I), but this had already disappeared by stage 45 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2K and L.

claim: Sostdc1 plays a persistent role within neuromasts in sterlet.
source: These data suggest Sostdc1 plays a persistent role within neuromasts, but any function in ampullary organ development is likely to be transient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Sostdc1 expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Any function of Sostdc1 in ampullary organ development is likely to be transient in sterlet.
source: These data suggest Sostdc1 plays a persistent role within neuromasts, but any function in ampullary organ development is likely to be transient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Sostdc1 expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Apcdd1 (adenomatosis polyposis coli down-regulated 1) is a secreted inhibitor of both the Bmp and Wnt pathways.
source: Apcdd1 (adenomatosis polyposis coli down-regulated 1) is also a secreted inhibitor of both the Bmp and Wnt pathways (Vonica et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Apcdd1 was 2.2-fold enriched in late-larval paddlefish operculum versus fin tissue.
source: Apcdd1 was 2.2-fold enriched in late-larval paddlefish operculum versus fin tissue (Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: At stage 36, Apcdd1 was not expressed in differentiated neuromast lines in sterlet.
source: At stage 36, Apcdd1 was not expressed in differentiated neuromast lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B), in contrast to Sostdc1 at the same stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: At stage 36, there was some Apcdd1 expression in the region of the preopercular neuromast line, as well as outside the lateral line system: at the edge of the operculum, near the future barbel region and around the mouth in sterlet.
source: However, there was some Apcdd1 expression in the region of the preopercular neuromast line, as well as outside the lateral line system: at the edge of the operculum, near the future barbel region and around the mouth (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: At stage 38, more diffuse Apcdd1 expression was seen in broader regions in sterlet.
source: At stage 38, more diffuse Apcdd1 expression was seen in broader regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: By stage 40, Apcdd1 expression was visible around ampullary organ primordia and some neuromasts on the head in sterlet.
source: By stage 40, expression was visible around ampullary organ primordia and some neuromasts on the head (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and F), as well as primI and primII on the trunk and a relatively short line of trailing cells behind primI (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and F.

claim: At stage 40, Apcdd1 expression was seen in primI and primII on the trunk and a relatively short line of trailing cells behind primI in sterlet.
source: By stage 40, expression was visible around ampullary organ primordia and some neuromasts on the head (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and F), as well as primI and primII on the trunk and a relatively short line of trailing cells behind primI (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3G.

claim: By stage 42, Apcdd1 expression on the head had largely resolved to the periphery of ampullary organs and neuromasts in sterlet.
source: By stage 42, Apcdd1 expression on the head had largely resolved to the periphery of ampullary organs and neuromasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H and I; compare with stage 42 Sox2 expression in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and J) and continued in the migrating primordia on the trunk and the short line of trailing cells behind primI (Figure 3—figure supplement 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3H and I.

claim: At stage 42, Apcdd1 expression continued in the migrating primordia on the trunk and the short line of trailing cells behind primI in sterlet.
source: By stage 42, Apcdd1 expression on the head had largely resolved to the periphery of ampullary organs and neuromasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H and I; compare with stage 42 Sox2 expression in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I and J) and continued in the migrating primordia on the trunk and the short line of trailing cells behind primI (Figure 3—figure supplement 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3J.

claim: At stage 45, Apcdd1 expression pattern largely persisted, although it seemed to be fading in the ventral infraorbital field in sterlet.
source: At stage 45, this expression pattern largely persisted, although it seemed to be fading in the ventral infraorbital field (Figure 3—figure supplement 3K and L) and faint expression was also now seen along the main body line, potentially at the periphery of trunk neuromasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 3M; compare with stage 45 Sox2 expression on the trunk in Figure 2—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3K and L.

claim: At stage 45, faint Apcdd1 expression was also seen along the main body line, potentially at the periphery of trunk neuromasts in sterlet.
source: At stage 45, this expression pattern largely persisted, although it seemed to be fading in the ventral infraorbital field (Figure 3—figure supplement 3K and L) and faint expression was also now seen along the main body line, potentially at the periphery of trunk neuromasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 3M; compare with stage 45 Sox2 expression on the trunk in Figure 2—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3M, and the location is inferred by comparison with Sox2 expression.

claim: The early, broad expression of Apcdd1 within ampullary organ fields and seemingly very late upregulation in neuromasts suggests that Apcdd1 may be more important for ampullary organ development in sterlet.
source: These data, especially the early, broad expression within ampullary organ fields and seemingly very late upregulation in neuromasts, suggest that Apcdd1 may be more important for ampullary organ development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Apcdd1 expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The pattern of Sostdc1 expression suggests its role may be more prominent during neuromast development in sterlet.
source: In contrast, the pattern of Sostdc1 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) suggests its role may be more prominent during neuromast development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Sostdc1 expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bmp5 was chosen as a target for CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis in G0-injected sterlet embryos owing to its earlier expression in ampullary organ primordia.
source: Having established that the Bmp signalling pathway is active throughout lateral line organ development and that genes encoding two Bmp ligands, a type II receptor and two secreted dual Bmp/Wnt antagonists are expressed, we wanted to explore the role of Bmp signalling in lateral line development. Bmp5 was chosen as a target for CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis in G0-injected sterlet embryos owing to its earlier expression in ampullary organ primordia.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: The sterlet genome has retained a high level of tetraploidy, including around 70% of ohnologs.
source: Analysis of this genome showed that, rather than being functionally diploid as previously thought (from microsatellite data; Ludwig et al., 2001), the sterlet genome has retained a high level of tetraploidy, including around 70% of ohnologs (i.e., gene paralogs resulting from the independent whole-genome duplication in the sterlet lineage) (Du et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Both Bmp5 ohnologs have been retained in the sterlet genome, on chromosomes 5 and 6, with 88.87% nucleotide identity in the coding sequence (and 95.60% amino acid identity).
source: Searching the reference genome (Vertebrate Genomes Project NCBI RefSeq assembly GCF_902713425.1) for Bmp5 showed that both Bmp5 ohnologs have been retained, on chromosomes 5 and 6, with 88.87% nucleotide identity in the coding sequence (and 95.60% amino acid identity).
evidence: This statement is supported by analysis of the sterlet reference genome.

claim: All of the Bmp5 sgRNAs fully match the ohnolog on chromosome 6.
source: All of our Bmp5 sgRNAs fully match the ohnolog on chromosome 6.
evidence: This statement is supported by analysis of the sterlet reference genome.

claim: Bmp5 sgRNAs 2 and 4 each have a single-base mismatch with the chromosome 5 ohnolog, respectively, in positions 7 and 4 of the target sequence (PAM-distal), which should be tolerated.
source: Relative to the ohnolog on chromosome 5, sgRNAs 2 and 4 (Table 1; Figure 4A) each have a single-base mismatch, respectively, in positions 7 and 4 of the target sequence (PAM-distal), which should be tolerated (Guo et al., 2014; Rabinowitz and Offen, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by analysis of the sterlet reference genome and citations to established literature about sgRNA tolerance of mismatches.

claim: Bmp5 sgRNA 1 has two mismatched bases (at positions 3 and 12 of the target sequence) with the chromosome 5 ohnolog.
source: However, our sgRNA 1 (Table 1; Figure 4A) has two mismatched bases (at positions 3 and 12 of the target sequence) and sgRNA 3 (Table 1; Figure 4A) has a single-base mismatch at position 20, adjacent to the PAM.
evidence: This statement is supported by analysis of the sterlet reference genome.

claim: Bmp5 sgRNA 3 has a single-base mismatch at position 20, adjacent to the PAM, with the chromosome 5 ohnolog.
source: However, our sgRNA 1 (Table 1; Figure 4A) has two mismatched bases (at positions 3 and 12 of the target sequence) and sgRNA 3 (Table 1; Figure 4A) has a single-base mismatch at position 20, adjacent to the PAM.
evidence: This statement is supported by analysis of the sterlet reference genome.

claim: All sgRNA mixtures are expected to have targeted both Bmp5 ohnologs, given that all combinations of injected sgRNAs contained either sgRNA 2 or sgRNA 4.
source: Therefore, although we expect all our sgRNAs to target the chromosome 6 ohnolog, it is possible that only sgRNAs 2 and 4 successfully target the chromosome 5 ohnolog (Guo et al., 2014; Rabinowitz and Offen, 2021). Nevertheless, given that all combinations of injected sgRNAs contained either sgRNA 2 or sgRNA 4 (Table 1; Supplementary file 1) we expect all mixtures to have targeted both Bmp5 ohnologs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sgRNA design and the known tolerance of mismatches.

claim: Relative to Tyr crispants (n=0/24), a mosaic reduction in Cacna1d expression in ampullary organ fields was observed in 46% of Bmp5 crispants (n=53/116).
source: Ampullary organ numbers in different fields vary considerably across individual larvae even in wild-types, but relative to Tyr crispants (n=0/24; Figure 4A and B; Supplementary file 1), we observed a mosaic reduction in Cacna1d expression in ampullary organ fields in 46% of Bmp5 crispants (n=53/116; Figure 4C–F; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4 and counting data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The efficacy of different Bmp5 sgRNA combinations varied significantly: injecting sgRNAs 2,3 led to fewer ampullary organs in 78% of cases (n=28/36) versus 39% for sgRNAs 1,2,3 (n=16/41) and 23% for sgRNAs 1,4 (n=9/39).
source: The efficacy of different sgRNA combinations varied significantly: injecting sgRNAs 2,3 led to fewer ampullary organs in 78% of cases (n=28/36; Supplementary file 1) versus 39% for sgRNAs 1,2,3 (n=16/41) and 23% for sgRNAs 1,4 (n=9/39; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by counting data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Of the 43 genotyped Bmp5 crispants, 33 had a positive 'knock-out' score, confirming successful disruption of the targeted gene.
source: Of the 43 genotyped crispants, 33 had a positive 'knock-out' score, confirming successful disruption of the targeted gene (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by genotyping data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The genotyping primers for Bmp5 only amplify the chromosome 6 ohnolog, owing to mismatches with the chromosome 5 ohnolog.
source: Our genotyping primers were designed before chromosome-level sterlet genomes were available; comparison with the reference genome (NCBI RefSeq assembly GCF_902713425.1) showed that only the chromosome 6 ohnolog can be amplified, owing to mismatches with the chromosome 5 ohnolog (primarily because the reverse primer targeted an intron).
evidence: This statement is supported by analysis of the sterlet reference genome.

claim: The ICE knock-out score was zero for ten Bmp5 crispants that nevertheless displayed the phenotype of reduced number of ampullary organs, which may be explained by the genotyping primers only amplifying the chromosome 6 ohnolog, combined with crispant mosaicism.
source: This, combined with crispant mosaicism, may explain why the ICE knock-out score was zero for ten Bmp5 crispants that nevertheless displayed the phenotype of reduced number of ampullary organs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genotyping data and the limitations of the genotyping approach.

claim: ISH for the electroreceptor-specific marker Kcnab3 confirmed the reduction in ampullary organ number in Bmp5 crispants relative to control Tyr crispants.
source: To examine the disruption in ampullary organ formation further, 15 control Tyr crispants and 13 Bmp5 crispants (six injected with sgRNAs 2,3 and seven injected with sgRNAs 1,4; Supplementary file 1) were subjected to ISH for the electroreceptor-specific marker Kcnab3 (Modrell et al., 2017a; Minařík et al., 2024a). Relative to control Tyr crispants (Figure 4G–I), this confirmed the reduction in ampullary organ number when there was no possibility of confusing the two sensory organ types (Figure 4J–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4G-L.

claim: Post-ISH Sox2 immunostaining revealed no obvious phenotype in the number and morphology of neuromasts in Bmp5 crispants.
source: The same Bmp5 crispants were then immunostained post-ISH for the supporting cell marker Sox2 (Hernández et al., 2007; Modrell et al., 2017a), which labels neuromasts more strongly than ampullary organs (Modrell et al., 2017a; Minařík et al., 2024a) and revealed no obvious phenotype in the number and morphology of neuromasts (Figure 4J1, K1 and L1; compare with Figure 4J, K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4J1, K1 and L1.

claim: Very few 'additional' ampullary organs appeared after Sox2 immunostaining in Bmp5 crispants, suggesting that disrupting the Bmp5 gene prevented ampullary organ formation, rather than blocking the later differentiation of Kcnab3-positive electroreceptors within ampullary organs.
source: Furthermore, very few 'additional' ampullary organs appeared after Sox2 immunostaining (Figure 4J1,K1 and L1; compare with Figure 4J, K and L), suggesting that disrupting the Bmp5 gene prevented ampullary organ formation, rather than blocking the later differentiation of Kcnab3-positive electroreceptors within ampullary organs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4J1, K1 and L1.

claim: Bmp5 crispants had significantly fewer ampullary organs overall than Tyr control crispants (p<0.0001).
source: Statistical analysis using a two-tailed Mann-Whitney (Wilcoxon rank sum) test revealed that Bmp5 crispants had significantly fewer ampullary organs overall than Tyr control crispants (p<0.0001; Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of counting data shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: All ampullary organ fields except for the dorsal supraorbital field had significantly fewer ampullary organs in Bmp5 crispants versus control Tyr crispants.
source: Indeed, all ampullary organ fields except for the dorsal supraorbital field (one of the smaller fields) had significantly fewer ampullary organs in Bmp5 crispants versus control Tyr crispants (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of counting data shown in Figure 5B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The dorsal supraorbital field originates from the anterodorsal lateral line placode.
source: The dorsal supraorbital field originates from the anterodorsal lateral line placode, which also gives rise to the ventral supraorbital and the dorsal and ventral infraorbital fields, all of which had significantly fewer ampullary organs in Bmp5 crispants versus control Tyr crispants (p=0.0008, p<0.0001 and p<0.0001, respectively; two-tailed Mann-Whitney test; Figure 5B).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature (Gibbs and Northcutt, 2004).

claim: The anterodorsal lateral line placode also gives rise to the ventral supraorbital and the dorsal and ventral infraorbital fields.
source: The dorsal supraorbital field originates from the anterodorsal lateral line placode, which also gives rise to the ventral supraorbital and the dorsal and ventral infraorbital fields, all of which had significantly fewer ampullary organs in Bmp5 crispants versus control Tyr crispants (p=0.0008, p<0.0001 and p<0.0001, respectively; two-tailed Mann-Whitney test; Figure 5B).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature (Gibbs and Northcutt, 2004).

claim: The ventral supraorbital, dorsal infraorbital, and ventral infraorbital fields all had significantly fewer ampullary organs in Bmp5 crispants versus control Tyr crispants (p=0.0008, p<0.0001 and p<0.0001, respectively).
source: The dorsal supraorbital field originates from the anterodorsal lateral line placode, which also gives rise to the ventral supraorbital and the dorsal and ventral infraorbital fields, all of which had significantly fewer ampullary organs in Bmp5 crispants versus control Tyr crispants (p=0.0008, p<0.0001 and p<0.0001, respectively; two-tailed Mann-Whitney test; Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of counting data shown in Figure 5B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The lack of effect in the dorsal supraorbital field may simply reflect the relatively small number of ampullary organs.
source: Thus, the lack of effect in the dorsal supraorbital field may simply reflect the relatively small number of ampullary organs (although this is not the smallest field).
evidence: This is speculation about the reason for the lack of a significant effect in the dorsal supraorbital field.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated targeting of Bmp5 in G0-injected embryos led to significantly fewer ampullary organs developing in almost all fields.
source: Overall, these data show that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated targeting of Bmp5 in G0-injected embryos led to significantly fewer ampullary organs developing in almost all fields.
evidence: This is a summary of the CRISPR/Cas9 data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Bmp5, which is expressed in ampullary organ primordia as well as in mature ampullary organs, normally acts to promote ampullary organ formation.
source: This suggests that Bmp5, which is expressed in ampullary organ primordia as well as in mature ampullary organs (Figure 1), normally acts to promote ampullary organ formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CRISPR/Cas9 data and the Bmp5 expression data.

claim: Stage 36 (newly hatched) sterlet yolk-sac larvae were treated with DMH1 for 20 hours, by which point (at 16 °C) they will have reached approximately stage 38.
source: We treated stage 36 (newly hatched) sterlet yolk-sac larvae with DMH1 for 20 hours, by which point (at 16 °C) they will have reached approximately stage 38: that is, just prior to the onset of ampullary organ development (ISH for Eya4 showed that ampullary organ primordia are present in all the main fields by stage 39; Minařík et al., 2024a).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: Stage 38 is just prior to the onset of ampullary organ development.
source: We treated stage 36 (newly hatched) sterlet yolk-sac larvae with DMH1 for 20 hours, by which point (at 16 °C) they will have reached approximately stage 38: that is, just prior to the onset of ampullary organ development (ISH for Eya4 showed that ampullary organ primordia are present in all the main fields by stage 39; Minařík et al., 2024a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous publication by the authors.

claim: ISH for Eya4 showed that ampullary organ primordia are present in all the main fields by stage 39.
source: We treated stage 36 (newly hatched) sterlet yolk-sac larvae with DMH1 for 20 hours, by which point (at 16 °C) they will have reached approximately stage 38: that is, just prior to the onset of ampullary organ development (ISH for Eya4 showed that ampullary organ primordia are present in all the main fields by stage 39; Minařík et al., 2024a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous publication by the authors.

claim: In comparison to DMSO controls (n=12), more ampullary organs had formed by stage 45 in all DMH1-treated larvae (n=17/17).
source: In comparison to DMSO controls (n=12), more ampullary organs had formed by stage 45 in all DMH1-treated larvae (n=17/17), as visualised by ISH for the hair cell/electroreceptor marker Cacna1d (Figure 6A–D; n=8) or for electroreceptor-specific Kcnab3 (Figure 6E–H; n=9).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6A-H.

claim: The increase in ampullary organ number in DMH1-treated larvae was most striking in the dorsalmost ampullary organ fields, i.e., the dorsal supraorbital, dorsal otic and supratemporal fields.
source: The increase in ampullary organ number seemed to be general but was most striking in the dorsalmost ampullary organ fields, i.e., the dorsal supraorbital, dorsal otic and supratemporal fields.
evidence: This is an observation based on the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In DMH1-treated larvae, there were so many ampullary organs in the dorsalmost fields that the fields appeared to fuse together in a line.
source: These fields were clearly separate in the DMSO control larvae (Figure 6A, B, E and F). However, in the DMH1-treated larvae, there were so many ampullary organs that the fields appeared to fuse together in a line (Figure 6C, D, G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6C, D, G and H.

claim: ISH for Cacna1d showed that the three dorsal ampullary organ fields were still clearly separate even in much older larvae.
source: ISH for Cacna1d showed that the three dorsal ampullary organ fields were still clearly separate even in much older larvae (Figure 6I and J), suggesting that the supernumerary ampullary organs in this region of DMH1-treated larvae at stage 45 were ectopic, rather than precocious.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: The supernumerary ampullary organs in the dorsalmost region of DMH1-treated larvae at stage 45 were ectopic, rather than precocious.
source: ISH for Cacna1d showed that the three dorsal ampullary organ fields were still clearly separate even in much older larvae (Figure 6I and J), suggesting that the supernumerary ampullary organs in this region of DMH1-treated larvae at stage 45 were ectopic, rather than precocious.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: The Cacna1d expression pattern in several DMH1-treated larvae suggested the presence of ectopic offshoots of the supraorbital neuromast line (n=5/8).
source: Although the increased number of ampullary organs in the dorsal fields was the most obvious and consistent phenotype, the Cacna1d expression pattern in several larvae suggested the presence of ectopic offshoots of the supraorbital neuromast line (Figure 6K and L; n=5/8).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6K and L.
